title: Longest Common Prefix
summary: Return the longest prefix shared by every string in the array, or "".
statement:
Return the longest string that is a prefix of every string in `strs`. If they share no prefix, return `""`.

For example `["dog","racecar","car"]` share no first letter, so the answer there is `""`.
hints: The common prefix can be no longer than the shortest string.
Compare column by column: check the character at position i in every string, and stop at the first mismatch or the end of any string.
Alternatively, start with the first string as the prefix and shorten it until every other string starts with it.
explain: All three words start with "fl", but the third letters differ ("o" in flower and flow, "i" in flight). So the answer is "fl".

title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
summary: Build a Trie with insert(word), search(word) (exact match) and startsWith(prefix).

perf.label: 30,000 inserts and 60,000 queries
perf.call: Trie t = new Trie(); long sum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 30000; i++) t.insert(BCB.str(BCB.rnd(5, 20), "abcde")); for (int i = 0; i < 30000; i++) { if (t.search(BCB.str(BCB.rnd(1, 10), "abcde"))) sum++; if (t.startsWith(BCB.str(BCB.rnd(1, 8), "abcde"))) sum += 2; } Object r = sum;

statement:
Implement a trie (prefix tree) for lowercase words:

- `Trie()` creates an empty trie,
- `void insert(String word)` adds a word,
- `boolean search(String word)` returns whether exactly that word was inserted,
- `boolean startsWith(String prefix)` returns whether any inserted word starts with `prefix`.

The tests call the class with a list of operations and their arguments.
constraints: Words and prefixes have only lowercase English letters
hints: Each node represents a prefix; its children are the possible next letters.
Give each node a Node[26] children array and a boolean marking whether a word ends there.
search and startsWith both walk down letter by letter; the only difference is that search also requires the end-of-word mark.
explain: After inserting "apple", searching "apple" is true but searching "app" is false, because "app" was never inserted as a whole word; startsWith("app") is true. After inserting "app", searching "app" becomes true. Constructors and inserts return `null`, so the output is `[null,null,true,false,true,null,true]`.

title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
summary: WordDictionary supports addWord(word) and search(word), where "." in the search word matches any single letter.

perf.label: 20,000 words and 20,000 wildcard searches
perf.call: WordDictionary d = new WordDictionary(); long sum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 20000; i++) d.addWord(BCB.str(BCB.rnd(3, 10), "abcd")); for (int i = 0; i < 20000; i++) { char[] w = BCB.str(BCB.rnd(3, 10), "abcd").toCharArray(); w[0] = '.'; if (d.search(new String(w))) sum++; } Object r = sum;

statement:
Design `WordDictionary`:

- `void addWord(String word)` adds a word,
- `boolean search(String word)` returns whether some added word matches `word`, where each `.` in `word` matches any single letter.

The tests call the class with a list of operations and their arguments.
constraints: Added words have only lowercase letters
Search words have lowercase letters and at most 2 dots
hints: Store the words in a trie, as in "Implement Trie".
Searching a normal letter follows one child. A "." can match any child, so you must try each of them.
Write search recursively over (node, index). For ".", return true if any child succeeds; at the end of the word, check the end-of-word mark.
explain: "pad" was never added, so it is false. "bad" was added. ".ad" matches "bad", "dad" or "mad", and "b.." matches "bad". So the output is `[null,null,null,null,false,true,true,true]`.

title: Replace Words
summary: Replace every word in the sentence that starts with a dictionary root by the shortest such root, and return the sentence.

in: "the cattle was rattled by the battery"
tests.out: "the cat was rat by the bat"

in: "ac cctac t cctatc at cat cctt cct t tc"
tests.out: "ac cct t cct at cat cct cct t tc"

in: "bbb ba baabb baab bab ba ab"
tests.out: "b b b b b b ab"

in: "ca cbbcaa acba a aca cb abaab bb"
tests.out: "c c a a a c a b"

in: "ataaaa ctta ctca ct tctc tt ctt ta"
tests.out: "ataaaa ctt ctca ct t t ctt t"

in: "abaa bbb ababab b b aab abab bbab abba bb"
tests.out: "a b a b b a a b a b"

in: "caata ttac cacta a caaccc caa caact ca c caac"
tests.out: "caa ttac cacta a caa caa caa ca c caa"

in: "aca b abb b acacc ab acb acbc"
tests.out: "a b a b a a a a"

in: "cacta ttt c cacca ta cact cata cac ccacaa cact ctca"
tests.out: "cac ttt c cac ta cac cata cac ccacaa cac ctca"

in: "tctct c c tac ca ta at taac ta"
tests.out: "tctct c c ta ca ta at ta ta"

perf.label: 1,000 roots and a 100,000-word sentence
perf.gen: List<String> a0 = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) a0.add(BCB.str(BCB.rnd(1, 5), "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz")); StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); for (int i = 0; i < 100000; i++) { if (i > 0) sb.append(' '); sb.append(BCB.str(BCB.rnd(3, 10), "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz")); } String a1 = sb.toString();

statement:
A root is a word that can be followed by more letters to form a longer word (`"cat"` + `"tle"` = `"cattle"`). Given the roots in `dictionary` and a `sentence` of words separated by single spaces, replace every word that starts with some root by the shortest such root.

Words that start with no root stay as they are. Return the new sentence.
constraints: All text is lowercase; sentence words are separated by single spaces
hints: For each word you need the shortest root that is a prefix of it.
Put the roots in a trie. Walk each word down the trie letter by letter.
Stop at the first node that ends a root and use that prefix; if you fall off the trie first, keep the whole word. Build the result with a StringBuilder.
explain: "cattle" starts with the root "cat", "rattled" with "rat" and "battery" with "bat", so each is replaced by its root. The other words have no root, giving "the cat was rat by the bat".

title: Search Suggestions System
summary: After each character of searchWord is typed, return up to three products (lexicographically smallest first) that start with the typed prefix.
statement:
You type `searchWord` one character at a time. After each character, suggest up to three products from `products` that start with what has been typed so far. If more than three match, pick the three that come first alphabetically.

Return a list with the suggestions after each character.
hints: Sorting the products puts every set of words with a common prefix into one contiguous block, already in alphabetical order.
For each prefix, binary-search the first product ≥ prefix and take up to three that still start with it.
A trie where each node keeps its three smallest words also works.
explain: After typing "m", "mo" and "mou" the matching products in alphabetical order begin with "mobile", "moneypot" and "monitor" for the first two, but only "mouse" and "mousepad" start with "mou". From then on, "mous" and "mouse" still match just those two. Each step lists at most three suggestions.

title: Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in an Array
summary: Return the maximum of nums[i] XOR nums[j] over all pairs (i may equal j) — in O(n) with a bitwise trie.

perf.label: n = 200,000
perf.gen: int[] a0 = new int[200000]; for (int i = 0; i < a0.length; i++) a0[i] = BCB.R.nextInt(Integer.MAX_VALUE);

statement:
Return the largest value of `nums[i] XOR nums[j]` over all pairs `0 ≤ i ≤ j < n` (so pairing a number with itself, which gives 0, is allowed).

Trying every pair is O(n²); aim for O(n · 31).

Insert the numbers bit by bit into a binary trie, highest bit first. For each number, walk the trie choosing the opposite bit whenever it exists, which builds the best partner greedily.
hints: To make the XOR large, you want the highest bits to differ.
Insert every number into a binary trie, from bit 30 down to bit 0.
For each number, walk the trie preferring the opposite bit at every level. Each time you can take it, that bit is set in the XOR. Keep the best result.
explain: 5 is 00101 in binary and 25 is 11001. They differ in the top three bits, so 5 XOR 25 = 11100 = 28, the largest of any pair.

title: Word Search II
summary: Return every word from the list that can be traced on the letter grid through horizontally or vertically adjacent cells, using each cell at most once per word. Any order.

perf.label: a 12×12 board and 30,000 words
perf.gen: char[][] a0 = BCB.charGrid(12, 12, "abcde"); Set<String> ws = new LinkedHashSet<>(); while (ws.size() < 30000) ws.add(BCB.str(BCB.rnd(1, 10), "abcde")); String[] a1 = ws.toArray(new String[0]);

statement:
`board` is a grid of lowercase letters. Return every word in `words` that can be spelled by a path of cells, moving up, down, left or right, without using any cell twice in the same word.

The words are distinct. Return them in any order.
hints: Running "Word Search" once per word repeats almost the same DFS thousands of times.
Put all the words in a trie and run one DFS from each cell, following the trie as you go. Stop as soon as the path is not a prefix of any word.
Store the full word at its end node, record it when you reach it and clear it so it is not reported twice. Pruning leaves you have finished makes it much faster.
explain: "oath" can be traced from the top-left "o" down and across neighbouring cells, and "eat" can be traced on the right side. "pea" has no "p" on the board, and "rain" cannot be connected, so the answer is `["oath","eat"]`.

title: Extra Characters in a String
summary: Split s into non-overlapping pieces that are dictionary words, leaving some characters unused. Return the minimum number of characters left over.
statement:
Break `s` into one or more **non-overlapping** substrings so that each substring is a word in `dictionary`. Some characters of `s` may not belong to any chosen substring; these are **extra** characters.

Return the minimum possible number of extra characters.
constraints: `s` and `dictionary[i]` have only lowercase English letters
hints: At each position i you either leave s[i] as an extra character, or start a dictionary word there. That suggests a recursion f(i) = fewest extras in s[i..].
f(i) = min(1 + f(i + 1), f(j) for every dictionary word s[i..j)). Memoise it, or fill dp from the end of the string backwards.
Checking every substring against a hash set costs O(n³) overall. Walking a trie from position i finds every word that starts at i in one pass, giving O(n² + total dictionary length).
explain: Take "leet" (indices 0–3) and "code" (indices 5–8). Only the "s" at index 4 is not covered, so the answer is 1.
